Syndication, redux

Project 34 · lesson four, read again after the coven learned to audit, lend and rival · index

The one sentence. Syndication is carrying one ledger’s history into another on a fixed interval, chained by hash, and the only check that matters is the one the receiving side can recompute itself.

What the first pass said

Lesson four in the HEZE slides makes three claims. The carry happens every six months whether or not anything was signed, so silence is provable too. Each checkpoint hashes what it carried together with the previous checkpoint, so forging one means forging every later one. And the far side reconciles at a scale that makes any single door invisible. The note at the bottom is the part that survives a second reading: a checkpoint you cannot recompute is a claim, and verifying a crossing means holding both chains and recomputing the source’s own Merkle root at the exact sequence the checkpoint names.

What changed between the passes

Since that slide was written, the coven gained real syndicate-to-syndicate interaction: a syndicate can audit a neighbour, lend to one, or rival one, and presidents and kings can interfere from above. That changes what syndication is for. In the first pass the carry crossed to “the other world’s chain”, a far side that reconciles without comment. In the second pass, the neighbours are near, they have motives, and an audit is nothing but a syndication run in the other direction on demand: hold both chains, recompute the root, compare.

audit

An audit is an unscheduled crossing with no carry. The auditor recomputes the neighbour’s root at a named sequence and either matches the neighbour’s published checkpoint or does not. Nothing moves; something is learned.

lend

A loan is a carry with a return date. The lender’s doors sign units across; the borrower’s checkpoint must include them; the next scheduled syndication proves either the repayment or its absence. The interval is the collateral.

rival

A rivalry is two syndicates publishing checkpoints about the same period and daring each other to recompute. The chain that cannot be recomputed loses standing, not units. Kings interfere by demanding the recompute early.

The three attacks, named

  1. The forged root. A checkpoint whose hash does not equal the hash of the events it claims. Caught by recomputing the source root. This is the templated attack the design was tested against, and it is the one that has actually cost real money elsewhere — bridges have lost hundreds of millions to roots nobody on the receiving side checked.
  2. The omitted interval. A syndicate that skips a quiet six months and later claims it was quiet. Caught because the checkpoint for the quiet interval is still taken and still chained; its absence is a break in the chain, not a gap in the diary.
  3. The rewritten past. A syndicate that edits an old event after carrying it. Caught by the chaining: the old checkpoint’s hash is inside every checkpoint after it, and the far side holds those.

What the design does not catch, and the first pass did not say: a syndicate that signs a false event correctly, carries it correctly, and chains it correctly. Syndication proves that what was said was said; it does not prove that it was true. That is the audit’s job, and the audit only works if the auditor can see the doors, not just the roots.

Redux: the rules, tightened

RuleFirst passSecond pass
Intervalevery six months, alwaysevery six months, always — plus on demand, when audited or lent to, without moving the scheduled one
CheckpointSHA-256 over events and previous checkpointsame, and the checkpoint names the exact door sequence it covers, so a recompute has a fixed target
Verificationfar side reconciles at scaleany holder of both chains recomputes; neighbours are expected to; kings may demand it early
Failurea break in the chaina break in the chain, recorded by whoever found it, in their own chain, so the finding is itself carried
What it provesthat the history crossed intactthat the history crossed intact — and nothing about whether the history was honest

Incognito: why a hidden syndicate is bad

The coven has a hidden attribute on a syndicate, and the question that follows is whether a hidden syndicate can take part in syndication at all. It cannot, and the reason is the same sentence as before. A hidden syndicate publishes checkpoints whose doors nobody else can see, so nobody can recompute its root; every checkpoint it carries is a claim, and the interval proves nothing about it. Its neighbours cannot audit it, cannot safely lend to it, and can rival it only by refusing to carry it, which is the correct move. A syndicate that wants to be carried has to be seen at the doors, not merely at the roots.

The same rule turned inside out is why “a hidden syndicate was behind it” is a bad explanation of history: it is a checkpoint with no doors. Project 55 applies that to the question of who funded communism, where the documented funders are a textile mill, a friend, the German Foreign Office and two rival states, and the hidden syndicate is the one part of the story that cannot be recomputed and never could.

Where this lands in the ship

The lesson lives in templates-heze/syndication.json, woven by the bridge. The coven’s relation templates (templates-relation/audit.json, lend.json, rival.json) are the second pass in code. This page is the second pass in prose, and the recommendation is small: the syndication slide should say, in its note, that the recompute is also the audit, so that a reader who only sees the slide knows the near side exists.
